meta.title: Burmese B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Burmese → English (see the Burmese, recall the meaning) and English → Burmese (see an English meaning, recall the Burmese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in his/her field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Burmese, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 103 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the everyday one-syllable verbs a frequency count cannot reach (taking, mixing, crossing, touching, hitting, catching, digging, burning, saving, avoiding, owning, leaning, sewing, kicking ...), the things of the house and the workshop, the body, materials and measures, and the faith — and the other 1397 are the commonest remaining words of the Burmese Wikipedia. Burmese writes no spaces between words, so that text was cut into words against the dictionary, and only words of two syllables or more are taken from the count (a one-syllable count also holds every piece the cut could not place). Burmese has two registers, the written and the spoken. The literary particles were taught at B1; this level goes on with the written vocabulary of the Burmese Wikipedia, encyclopaedic in places (government, history, religion, science), and its own short list carries the everyday one-syllable verbs and nouns that a count of written text cannot reach. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here. Every word is in the Myanmar script, as Burmese is written; the Alphabet deck, first in this collection, teaches the letters and the tone marks. Beneath each word is its pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet, as Wiktionary gives it, with the four tones marked: à low, á high, a̰ creaky, aʔ checked (short, with a catch). Many short Burmese words are several words in one spelling, so a card shows the meanings of the part of speech it teaches (ကို, the object particle; ငါး, five and fish). A noun shows the classifier it is counted with where Wiktionary names one. Example sentences are few: 76 of the 1500 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about 590 Burmese sentences; none is invented. There is no speaker button: few devices have a Burmese voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, pronunciation and classifiers: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Burmese Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
